\">\u003cfigcaption>Figure · page 37\u003c/figcaption>\u003c/figure>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Medication Review and Risk Factor Modification\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Post-endoscopic management also includes removal of precipitating factors.\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 38\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Patients should avoid: NSAIDs, alcohol, smoking, and unnecessary anticoagulants if\u003cbr>possible. If anticoagulation is required: bleeding risk, thrombosis risk, and timing of re-\u003cbr>initiation must be carefully reassessed. Alcohol cessation is critically important in: Alcoholic\u003cbr>liver disease because continued alcohol intake accelerates:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">cirrhosis progression,    portal hypertension,    recurrent bleeding,    and liver failure.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Nutritional Support Patients with chronic liver disease are commonly: Protein-energy\u003cbr>malnourished Therefore nutritional optimization is essential.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Management includes: adequate calories, balanced protein intake, vitamin supplementation,\u003cbr>and correction of micronutrient deficiencies.  Contrary to older teaching: Severe protein\u003cbr>restriction is usually avoided because it worsens catabolism and sarcopenia.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Surveillance and Long-Term Follow-Up\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Most guidelines recommend: Ultrasound ± AFP every 6 months for HCC surveillance.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Long-Term Prevention of Upper Gastrointestinal Bleeding\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Long-term prevention is the final and one of the most important phases in the management of\u003cbr>upper gastrointestinal bleeding because many patients remain at high risk of:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">The prevention strategy depends mainly on whether the bleeding was:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  variceal,   •  or non-variceal.\u003c/p>\u003cfigure class=\"note-figure\">\u003cimg loading=\"lazy\" alt=\"Illustration associated with page 38\" src=\"data:image/webp;base64,\">\u003cfigcaption>Figure · page 38\u003c/figcaption>\u003c/figure>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 39\u003c/div>\u003cfigure class=\"note-figure\">\u003cimg loading=\"lazy\" alt=\"Illustration associated with page 39\" src=\"data:image/webp;base64,\">\u003cfigcaption>Figure · page 39\u003c/figcaption>\u003c/figure>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Prevention of Recurrent Variceal Bleeding\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Patients who survive a: Variceal hemorrhage have a very high risk of recurrent bleeding if\u003cbr>preventive measures are not implemented. According to hepatology studies, recurrent\u003cbr>variceal hemorrhage commonly occurs within 1–2 years if secondary prophylaxis is not\u003cbr>given. Therefore, all patients with variceal bleeding require:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Secondary prevention\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Repeat Endoscopic Variceal Ligation (EVL) The cornerstone of long-term prevention is:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Repeat EVL Band ligation sessions are repeated every:2–4 weeks until: Complete variceal\u003cbr>obliterations achieved. The reason repeated sessions are necessary is because:\u003c/p>\u003cfigure class=\"note-figure\">\u003cimg loading=\"lazy\" alt=\"Illustration associated with page 39\" src=\"data:image/webp;base64,
